opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really useful frame. If you look at what humans actually learn from, very little of it is "raw" data from the world. Most of what any individual absorbs is stuff that other humans generated: stories, explanations, textbooks, arguments, songs, proofs. In a sense, that's all synthetic data. It's a compressed, curated output of other minds that have already done some processing on reality.

The interesting thing is that it doesn't just recycle. Each generation takes the corpus it inherited, does some exploration against the real world or against internal consistency, and then writes back a slightly better version. Someone tries an idea, it fails or succeeds, and the successful version gets written down and taught. So you have this loop of generation, then a filter or verifier, then distillation into the next generation's training data. That's very close to how we think about self-improvement in models: sample a lot, keep what checks out, train on it, repeat.

The key ingredient is the verifier. People worry about model collapse, where you train on your own outputs and drift into mush. Human culture mostly avoided that because there was a grounding signal. Did the bridge stay up? Did the crop grow? Did the proof hold? Did people actually find the story moving? Without those checks you get things like folk beliefs that persist for centuries. With strong checks, like in mathematics or engineering, you get really fast compounding progress.

So when I think about AI, the question becomes: where do we have good verifiers? In code and math we have very crisp ones, and that's exactly where we're seeing the most rapid gains from RL and synthetic data. In fuzzier domains, the signal is noisier, and humans took a long time there too. Culture is basically a very long-running, very distributed version of the same algorithm, and it's slow because the feedback loops ran on human lifetimes. Models can potentially run that loop much faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes culture as a feedback loop of generated knowledge, verification, and learning across generations, but does not mention human genetic evolution or coevolution with cultural learning.

r002.rationale: It identifies real-world outcomes—such as whether a bridge stays up or crops grow—as grounding checks that verify cultural knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing that I find most useful here is that humans are actually a pretty striking example of how far you can get on synthetic data, and we don't usually think of it that way.

If you look at a single human in isolation, the amount of raw sensory data we get from the world is enormous, but the amount of actual supervised signal about how to do things well is tiny. Most of what makes a person capable isn't learned from direct contact with reality. It's learned from other people. Language, maths, how to build a boat, which plants are poisonous, how to reason about causality. Almost none of that was discovered by the individual. It was distilled over many generations and handed to them in compressed form.

And that compressed form is really a kind of synthetic data. It's not the raw experience. It's a curated, filtered, error-corrected summary of experience that someone else had, or that a whole lineage of people had. Culture is the process of taking expensive real-world trial and error, running a verifier over it, which is basically "did this person survive, did this work, did the community keep doing it," and then emitting a much cheaper, much denser artifact that the next generation can train on.

The thing I find interesting is how similar that loop is to what we do when we train models on model-generated data. You have some generator that produces candidate solutions. You have some way of checking them, whether that's the world pushing back or a formal verifier or just peer judgement. You keep the good ones and you throw away the bad ones, and then the filtered set becomes the training distribution for the next round. Every generation's output is the next generation's input. Humans have been doing exactly that with stories, apprenticeship, textbooks, and so on, for tens of thousands of years.

What's different is the bottleneck. In human cultural evolution, the expensive step was always the generation and the filtering. You needed a person to live a whole life to produce a small number of useful lessons, and the lossy channel between brains meant most of it got dropped. The transmission was cheap relative to that, but still slow. With models, generation is suddenly almost free, and the question becomes entirely about the quality of your verifier and how much signal you can extract per unit of compute. That's why I think so much of the action right now is in environments and reward, not in architecture.

There's also a cautionary side. Cultural evolution isn't guaranteed to go anywhere good. You can have cultures that accumulate very confident, very internally consistent bodies of knowledge that are just wrong, because the feedback loop with reality got weak. Model collapse is the same failure mode. If you train on your own outputs without something external grounding them, you drift towards whatever is easiest to generate and easiest to accept, rather than what's true. The societies that made progress fastest were the ones that kept a tight loop with the physical world, with experiment, with trade, with things that could tell you no. I think that's the main lesson I take from the analogy: synthetic data works, humans are the proof, but only to the extent that something in the loop is actually in contact with ground truth.

r001.rationale: The response describes culture passing filtered knowledge between generations, but does not mention genetic evolution or a coevolutionary loop between genes and culture.

r002.rationale: It identifies the physical world’s feedback—whether a practice works or helps people survive—as a verifier for cultural knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think human culture is, in a pretty literal sense, a process of learning from data generated by other intelligences. You read a textbook, and that’s not raw experience of the world. It’s the output of a human who has taken their experience, combined it with what they’ve learned from other humans, and distilled it into something you can learn from much more efficiently.

And that process compounds. A scientist spends years figuring something out, writes it down, and then the next generation can learn it in an afternoon. They don’t have to rediscover everything from scratch. A huge amount of what makes us capable comes from this accumulated material, rather than from each individual’s ability to independently work things out.

But the crucial thing is that there’s some selection happening. We generate explanations, arguments, theories, and then we test them against the world or against other people’s criticism. Some of those ideas survive and get taught. Others disappear. It isn’t just that we keep producing more text and therefore get smarter.

So when I think about synthetic data for AI, the interesting question is: can you reproduce that whole loop? Can a system explore, discover something, check whether it’s right, and then turn that discovery into training material that makes the next system better? Human culture seems like a pretty strong demonstration that learning from the outputs of other learners can take you a very long way—provided you have mechanisms for preserving useful discoveries and correcting mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response describes cultural knowledge accumulating across generations, but does not mention genetic evolution or a coevolutionary feedback loop between genetic evolution and cultural learning.

r002.rationale: It says explanations and theories are tested against the world, and useful ideas survive while others disappear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is that most of what any individual learns isn’t coming directly from interacting with the world. It’s coming from the outputs of other humans. You read a textbook, listen to an explanation, study somebody’s proof. That’s data generated by other intelligences, and it lets you acquire capabilities without rediscovering everything yourself.

And those outputs can be much better learning material than the raw experience that produced them. Someone spends twenty years figuring something out, and then writes an explanation you can understand in an afternoon. So culture is doing this enormous amount of computation and compressing the results into a form the next generation can learn from.

But the grounding matters. If everyone just repeats everyone else, you can propagate mistakes. The especially powerful loop is that people generate ideas, test them against the world, and then transmit the ones that work. Mathematics has proofs; engineering has things that either function or fail. You’re not relying solely on whether an explanation sounds convincing.

So when I think about learning from synthetic data, the interesting question isn’t just whether a model can learn from another model’s outputs. Humans do the analogous thing constantly. It’s how you build a process that produces useful new knowledge, checks it, and makes it easier for the next learner to acquire.

r001.rationale: The response describes cultural learning from human-generated outputs and testing ideas, but it does not mention human genetic evolution or a coevolutionary feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It says cultural ideas are tested against the world and that working engineering or mathematical proofs provide checks, communicating real-world agreement as verification.
